    MA3003 · HEAT TRANSFER

    Heat Conduction Equation

    #Fundamental Concepts

    #Coordinate Systems

    Heat transfer has both direction and magnitude.
    Thus, it is a vector quantity. Hence, a suitable coordinate system is required.

    Types of coordinate systems:

    • Rectangular coordinates (x,y,z)
    • Cylindrical coordinates (r,ϕ,z)
    • Spherical coordinates (r,ϕ,θ)

    #Steady vs Transient Heat Transfer

    Classification of heat transfer problems:

    • Steady — no change with time at any point
    • Transient — varies with time

    For steady-state heat transfer, temperature or heat flux remains unchanged with time at any location,
    but these quantities may vary from one location
    to another.

    #Multi-Dimensional Heat Transfer

    Generally, heat transfer through a medium is 3-dimensional. If the temperature
    in a medium varies in either two or one primary directions, it is said to be a 2D
    or 1D heat transfer respectively.

    Rewriting Fourier’s law of heat conduction,

    q˙​x​=−k∂x∂T​ q˙​y​=−k∂y∂T​ q˙​z​=−k∂z∂T​

    where each partial derivative corresponds to
    the temperature gradient along that direction

    Expressing the above as a vector equation,

    💡
    q˙​=−k∇T

    where ∇T=∂x∂T​i+∂y∂T​j+∂z∂T​k

    Consider an isothermal surface in a medium. The heat transfer vector at a point P on this surface must be perpendicular to the surface, and point
    in the direction of decreasing temperature.

    Rate of heat conduction at P is then,

    q˙​n​=−k∂n∂T​

    The rate of heat transfer can be resolved into
    the     x, y, and z directions, as shown above.

    #General Conduction Equation

    #Rectangular/Cartesian Coordinates

    Recall that the heat balance equation for a system is,

    E˙stored​=Q˙​in​−Q˙​out​+E˙gen​

    mc∂t∂T​=(Q˙​x​+Q˙​y​+Q˙​z​)−(Q˙​x+dx​+Q˙​y+dy​+Q˙​z+dz​)+e˙gen​(dxdydz)

    (ρ dxdydz)c∂t∂T​=(Q˙​x​+Q˙​y​+Q˙​z​)−(Q˙​x+dx​+Q˙​y+dy​+Q˙​z+dz​)+e˙gen​(dxdydz)

    Using Taylor series expansion and neglecting higher-order terms,

    Q˙​x+dx​=Q˙​x​+∂x∂Q˙​​dx+∂x2∂2Q˙​​(dx)2+∂x3∂3Q˙​​(dx)3+…

    Q˙​x+dx​=Q˙​x​+∂x∂Q˙​​dx

    Using Fourier’s law of heat conduction,

    Q˙​x​−Q˙​x+dx​=−∂x∂Q˙​​dx

    Q˙​x​−Q˙​x+dx​=−∂x∂​Q˙​ dx

    Q˙​x​−Q˙​x+dx​=−∂x∂​(−k∂x∂T​ dydz)dx

    Q˙​x​−Q˙​x+dx​=∂x∂​(k∂x∂T​)dxdydz

    Substituting into the heat balance equation,

    (ρ dxdydz)c∂t∂T​=[∂x∂​(k∂x∂T​)+∂y∂​(k∂y∂T​)+∂z∂​(k∂z∂T​)]dxdydz+e˙gen​(dxdydz)

    Simplifying the above gives the general equation for heat conduction.

    💡
    ρc∂t∂T​=∂x∂​(k∂x∂T​)+∂y∂​(k∂y∂T​)+∂z∂​(k∂z∂T​)+e˙gen​

    where e˙gen​ is heat generation per unit volume (W/m3)

    If thermal conductivity k is a constant,

    kρc​∂t∂T​=∂x2∂2T​+∂y2∂2T​+∂z2∂2T​+ke˙gen​​

    💡
    α1​∂t∂T​=∂x2∂2T​+∂y2∂2T​+∂z2∂2T​+ke˙gen​​

    where α=ρck​ is the thermal diffusivity of the material (how fast heat travels)

    #Cylindrical and Spherical Coordinates

    General heat conduction equation in cylindrical coordinates,

    💡
    ρc∂t∂T​=r1​∂r∂​(kr∂r∂T​)+r21​∂ϕ∂​(k∂ϕ∂T​)+∂z∂​(k∂z∂T​)+e˙gen​

    where heat flux has radial, circumferential, and axial components

    General heat conduction equation in spherical coordinates,

    💡
    ρc∂t∂T​=r21​∂r∂​(kr2∂r∂T​)+r2sin2θ1​∂ϕ∂​(k∂ϕ∂T​)+r2sinθ1​∂θ∂​(ksinθ∂θ∂T​)+e˙gen​

    where heat flux has radial, polar, and azimuthal components

    #Boundary and Initial Conditions

    The general heat conduction equation does not account for the thermal conditions
    on the surfaces of the medium. However, heat flux and temperature distribution in
    a medium depend on those conditions. Thus, we require boundary conditions.

    #Constant Surface Temperature

    For 1-dimensional heat transfer through a plane wall of thickness L, the specified temperature boundary conditions can be expressed as,

    T(0,t)=T1​

    T(L,t)=T2​

    #Constant Heat Flux

    Heat flux anywhere in the medium, including the boundaries, can be expressed by Fourier’s law of
    heat conduction.

    −k∂x∂T​​x=0​=q˙​s​

    For a properly insulated (adiabatic) surface, it can
    be modeled as a surface with a heat flux of zero.

    ∂x∂T​​x=0​=0

    On an insulated surface, temperature gradient in
    the direction normal to the surface is zero. Thus,
    the temperature function must be perpendicular
    to the surface since the slope is zero.

    Consider the two surfaces of a large hot plate
    of thickness L suspended vertically in air.

    Since both sides are subjected to the same thermal conditions, temperature distribution in each half is the same (thermal symmetry).

    At the plane of symmetry, ∂x∂T​=0.

    The center plane can be viewed as an insulated surface, with a similar boundary condition as
    the zero heat flux boundary condition.

    #Convection Boundary Condition

    The convection boundary condition is based on the surface energy balance.
    Heat conduction at a surface in a given direction must be equal to the heat
    convection at the surface in the same direction.

    Note that a surface has zero thickness, and thus no mass, and it cannot store
    any energy. Hence, the entire net heat entering the surface from one side
    must leave the surface from the other side.

    For 1-dimensional heat transfer in a plate
    of thickness L, boundary conditions are,

    −k∂x∂T​​x=0​=h1​[T∞1​​−T(0,t)]

    −k∂x∂T​​x=L​=h2​[T(L,t)−T∞2​​]

    where h are convection heat transfer coefficients,
    and     T∞​ are the temperatures of the surrounding
    fluid on the two sides of the plate

    #Radiation Boundary Condition

    Using energy balance, heat conduction at a surface in a given direction must
    be equal to the radiation exchange at the surface in the same direction.

    For 1-dimensional heat transfer in a plate
    of thickness L, boundary conditions are,

    −k∂x∂T​​x=0​=ε1​σ[Tsurr,1​4−T(0,t)4]

    −k∂x∂T​​x=L​=ε2​σ[T(L,t)4−Tsurr,2​4]

    where ε are emissivity of the boundary surfaces,
    and     Tsurr​ are the average temperatures of the surfaces surrounding the two sides of the plate

    #Interface Boundary Condition

    Boundary conditions at an interface is such that:

    • Two bodies in contact must have the same temperature at the interface
    • Heat flux on two sides of an interface must be the same

    The boundary conditions at the interface of two bodies in perfect contact can be expressed as,

    TA​(x0​,t)=TB​(x0​,t)

    −kA​∂x∂TA​​​x=x0​​=−kB​∂x∂TB​​​x=x0​​

    where k are thermal conductivities of the layers

    #Phase Change Boundary Condition

    Consider a block of ice melting into water, heat flux at the boundary of ice and water is not equal, as some heat is used to melt the ice.

    −k∂x∂T​​u​−(−k∂x∂T​​s​)=m˙′′(hs​−hu​)

    k∂x∂T​​s​=k∂x∂T​​u​+m˙′′hfs​

    where m˙′′ is mass flux with units kg/m2⋅s,
    and     hfs​ is enthalpy of fusion of ice

    #Generalized Boundary Condition

    In general, a surface may involve convection, radiation, and specified heat flux simultaneously. The boundary condition for these combined conditions is then,

    💡
    ​Heat Transferto the surfacein all modes​​=​Heat Transferfrom the surfacein all modes​​

    #Example 1

    Assumptions:

    • Steady-state heat transfer
    • 1-dimensional heat transfer, A≫L
    • Constant thermal conductivity k
    • No heat generation in the base plate
    • Upper part of iron is well-insulated, thus
      all heat generated in the resistance wire
      is transferred to the base plate

    Inner surface of base plate is subjected to uniform heat flux.

    q˙​0​=AQ˙​​=0.31200​=40 kW/m2

    Applying the general conduction equation to the base plate,

    α1​∂t∂T​=∂x2∂2T​+∂y2∂2T​+∂z2∂2T​+ke˙gen​​

    ∂x2∂2T​=0

    Since it is a steady-state conduction, the term on the LHS is zero. Assuming only
    1D heat transfer in the     x-direction, heat transfer in the y- and z-directions are
    negligible. No heat is generated in the base plate, thus     e˙gen​=0.

    Solving the conduction equation,

    dxdT​=C1​

    T(x)=C1​x+C2​

    Solutions are obtained by integrating twice.

    Boundary condition of inner surface,

    q˙​0​=−kdxdT​​x=0​=40 kW/m2

    Heat flux from resistance wire is equal
    to heat conduction at the inner surface.

    Boundary condition of outer surface,

    −kdxdT​​x=L​=h[T(L)−T∞​]

    Heat conduction at outer surface is equal to
    heat convection to the surrounding fluid (air).

    Evaluating the constants

    Substituting into the 1st boundary condition,

    q˙​0​=−kC1​ → C1​=−kq˙​0​​

    Note that dxdT​ is a constant and independent of x.

    Substituting into the 2nd boundary condition,

    −kC1​=h[C1​L+C2​−T∞​]

    Note that dxdT​ is a constant and independent of x.

    Solving for constant C2​,

    −k(−kq˙​0​​)=h[−kq˙​0​L​+C2​−T∞​]

    C2​=T∞​+hq˙​0​​+kq˙​0​L​

    Evaluating the temperatures

    Substituting C1​ and C2​ into T(x),

    T(x)=−kq˙​0​​x+T∞​+hq˙​0​​+kq˙​0​L​

    T(x)=T∞​+q˙​0​(kL−x​+h1​)

    At the inner surface, where x=0,

    T(0)=293+40000(150.005​+801​)

    T(0)=806 K=533°C

    At the outer surface, where x=L,

    T(L)=293+40000(0+801​)

    T(L)=793 K=520°C

    #Example 2

    Assumptions:

    • Steady-state heat transfer
    • 1-dimensional heat transfer
    • Constant thermal conductivity k
    • No heat generation in engine housing
    • Inner surface subjected to constant q˙​0​

    Applying the general conduction equation,

    α1​∂t∂T​=∂x2∂2T​+∂y2∂2T​+∂z2∂2T​+ke˙gen​​

    dx2d2T​=0

    Solving the conduction equation,

    dxdT​=C1​

    T(x)=C1​x+C2​

    Boundary condition of inner surface,

    q˙​0​=−kdxdT​​x=0​=6 kW/m2

    Heat flux from the engine is equal to heat conduction at the inner surface.

    Boundary condition of outer surface,

    −kdxdT​​x=L​=h[T(L)−T∞​]

    Heat conduction from housing is equal
    to heat convection to surrounding fluid.

    Evaluating the constants,

    C1​=−kq˙​0​​

    C2​=T∞​+kq˙​0​​(hk​+L)

    Substituting into T(x),

    T(x)=T∞​+kq˙​0​​(hk​+L−x)

    Temperature of inner surface, where x=0,

    T(0)=308+13.56000​(2013.5​+0.01)

    T(0)=612 K=339°C

    Temperature of outer surface, where x=L,

    T(L)=308+13.56000​(2013.5​)

    T(L)=608 K=335°C

    The outer surface temperature of the engine housing is higher than the safe temperature of 200°C. Thus, the engine housing should be covered with a
    protective insulation to prevent a fire hazard in the event of oil leakage.

    #Example 3

    Assumptions:

    • Steady-state heat transfer
    • 1D heat transfer (thermal symmetry)
    • Constant thermal conductivity k
    • No heat generation

    The cylinder can be unfolded into a flat plate with both sides of the plate being
    exposed to the surroundings. Thus, there is thermal symmetry along the center
    plane; radius of the cylinder halfway between the inner and outer radius.

    Applying the general conduction equation,

    ρc∂t∂T​=r1​∂r∂​(kr∂r∂T​)+r21​∂ϕ∂​(k∂ϕ∂T​)+∂z∂​(k∂z∂T​)+e˙gen​

    r1​drd​(krdrdT​)=0

    drd​(rdrdT​)=0

    Solving the conduction equation,

    rdrdT​=C1​

    T(r)=C1​ ln(r)+C2​

    drdT​=rC1​​

    ∫dT=∫rC1​​ dr

    T(r)=C1​ ln(r)+C2​

    Boundary conditions,

    T(r1​)=T1​=150°C (inner surface)

    T(r2​)=T2​=60°C (outer surface)

    Substituting T(r1​) and T(r2​) into T(r),

    T1​=C1​ ln(r1​)+C2​

    T2​=C1​ ln(r2​)+C2​

    Solving the simultaneous equations,

    C1​=ln(r2​/r1​)T2​−T1​​

    C2​=T1​−ln(r2​/r1​)T2​−T1​​ ln(r1​)

    Equation for the variation of temperature,

    T(r)=ln(r2​/r1​)ln(r/r1​)​(T2​−T1​)+T1​

    Rate of heat loss from steam through the pipe,

    Q˙​=−kAdrdT​

    Q˙​=−k(2πrL)rC1​​

    Q˙​=−2πkLC1​

    Q˙​=2πkL[ln(r2​/r1​)T1​−T2​​]

    Q˙​=2π(20)(20)ln(0.08/0.06)150−60​

    Q˙​=786 kW

    #Heat Generation in a Solid

    Many practical heat transfer applications involve the conversion of some
    form of energy into thermal energy in the medium — heat generation.

    #Conduction in a Plane Wall

    Consider heat generation in a plane wall.

    Applying the heat conduction equation,

    α1​∂t∂T​=∂x2∂2T​+∂y2∂2T​+∂z2∂2T​+ke˙gen​​

    0=∂x2∂2T​+ke˙gen​​

    Steady-state, 1-dimensional heat transfer, where
    the material has constant thermal conductivity     k.

    Solving the above differential equation,

    ∫d2T=∫−ke˙gen​​ dx2

    dxdT​=−ke˙gen​​x+C1​

    ∫dT=∫−ke˙gen​​x+C1​ dx

    T(x)=−2ke˙gen​​x2+C1​x+C2​

    #Asymmetrical Boundary Conditions

    Boundary conditions of the plane wall are,

    T(−L)=T1​

    T(L)=T2​

    where T1​=T2​

    Substituting the boundary conditions,

    T(−L)=T1​=−2ke˙gen​​L2−C1​L+C2​

    T(L)=T2​=−2ke˙gen​​L2+C1​L+C2​

    Solving the simultaneous equations,

    C1​=2LT2​−T1​​

    C2​=2ke˙gen​​L2+2T1​+T2​​

    Temperature distribution across the plane wall is,

    T(x)=−2ke˙gen​​x2+2LT2​−T1​​x+2ke˙gen​​L2+2T1​+T2​​

    T(x)=2ke˙gen​​(L2−x2)+2LT2​−T1​​x+2T1​+T2​​

    💡
    T(x)=2ke˙gen​​L2(1−L2x2​)+2LT2​−T1​​x+2T1​+T2​​

    #Symmetrical Boundary Conditions

    Boundary conditions of the plane wall are,

    T(−L)=T(L)=Ts​

    dxdT​​x=0​=0

    Maximum temperature occurs at plane
    of symmetry, where     x=0. Thus, the
    temperature gradient is zero.

    Substituting the boundary conditions,

    dxdT​​x=0​=−ke˙gen​​(0)+C1​

    Ts​=−2ke˙gen​​L2+C2​

    Solving for the constants,

    C1​=0

    C2​=2ke˙gen​​L2+Ts​

    Temperature distribution across the plane wall is,

    💡
    T(x)=2ke˙gen​​L2(1−L2x2​)+Ts​

    Energy balance at the surface is,

    Q˙​cond​=Q˙​conv​

    −kdxdT​​x=L​=h(Ts​−T∞​)

    −k(−ke˙gen​​L)=h(Ts​−T∞​)

    💡
    Ts​=he˙gen​​L+T∞​

    Maximum temperature occurs at the plane of symmetry, where x=0.

    Tmax​=2ke˙gen​​L2(1−L20​)+Ts​

    Tmax​=2ke˙gen​​L2+Ts​

    💡
    Ts​=Tmax​−2ke˙gen​​L2

    #Adiabatic Boundary Condition

    Boundary conditions of the plane wall are,

    T(L)=Ts​

    dtdT​​x=0​=0

    On an insulated surface, temperature gradient in
    the direction normal to the surface is zero. Thus,
    the temperature function must be perpendicular
    to the surface since the slope is zero.

    Substituting the boundary conditions,

    dtdT​​x=0​=−2ke˙gen​​(0)+C1​

    Ts​=−2ke˙gen​​L2+C2​

    Solving for the constants,

    C1​=0

    C2​=2ke˙gen​​L2+Ts​

    Temperature distribution across the plane wall is,

    💡
    T(x)=2ke˙gen​​L2(1−L2x2​)+Ts​

    Energy balance at the surface is,

    Q˙​cond​=Q˙​conv​

    −kdxdT​​x=L​=h(Ts​−T∞​)

    −k(−ke˙gen​​L)=h(Ts​−T∞​)

    💡
    Ts​=he˙gen​​L+T∞​

    #Conduction in a Solid Cylinder

    Consider heat generation in a solid cylinder.

    Note that the cylinder is not hollow on the inside.

    Applying the heat conduction equation,

    0=r1​∂r∂​(kr∂r∂T​)+e˙gen​

    0=∂r∂​(r∂r∂T​)+ke˙gen​​r

    Steady-state, 1-dimensional heat transfer, where
    the material has constant thermal conductivity     k.

    Solving the above differential equation,

    ∫d(rdrdT​)=∫−ke˙gen​​r dr

    rdrdT​=−2ke˙gen​​r2+C1​

    drdT​=−2ke˙gen​​r+rC1​​

    Integrating the above equation,

    ∫dT=∫−2ke˙gen​​r+rC1​​ dr

    T(r)=−4ke˙gen​​r2+C1​ ln(r)+C2​

    Boundary conditions for the solid cylinder are,

    T(ro​)=Ts​

    drdT​​r=0​=0

    Centerline of the cylinder is the line of geometric symmetry.
    Thus, the temperature gradient at the centerline is zero.

    Solving for the constants,

    C1​=0

    C2​=4ke˙gen​​ro​2+Ts​

    Temperature distribution across the cylinder is,

    T(r)=−4ke˙gen​​r2+4ke˙gen​​ro​2+Ts​

    T(r)=4ke˙gen​​(ro​2−r2)+Ts​

    💡
    T(r)=4ke˙gen​​ro​2(1−ro​2r2​)+Ts​

    where ro​ is the outer radius of the cylinder, and r is the radius of interest

    Maximum temperature occurs at the line of symmetry, where r=0.

    Tmax​=4ke˙gen​​ro​2(1−ro​20​)+Ts​

    Tmax​=4ke˙gen​​ro​2+Ts​

    💡
    Ts​=Tmax​−4ke˙gen​​ro​2

    #Example

    Assumptions:

    • Steady-state heat transfer
    • 1-dimensional heat transfer
    • Constant thermal conductivities
    • Uniform heat generation in wire

    kwire​=15 W/m⋅K

    kceramic​=1.2 W/m⋅K

    e˙gen​=50 W/cm3=50×106 W/m3

    Let T1​ be the unknown temperature at the interface between wire and ceramic.

    Twire​=4ke˙gen​​(r1​2−r2)+T1​

    Tceramic​=ln(r2​/r1​)ln(r/r1​)​(Ts​−T1​)+T1​

    Note that for the ceramic layer, r1​≤r≤r2​.

    Conduction in the wire

    Applying the heat conduction equation,

    ρc∂t∂T​=r1​∂r∂​(kr∂r∂T​)+r21​∂ϕ∂​(k∂ϕ∂T​)+∂z∂​(k∂z∂T​)+e˙gen​

    0=r1​drd​(krdrdTwire​​)+e˙gen​

    0=drd​(rdrdTwire​​)+ke˙gen​​r

    Integrating once,

    ∫d(rdrdTwire​​)=∫−ke˙gen​​r dr

    rdrdTwire​​=−2ke˙gen​​r2+C1​

    Integrating twice,

    ∫dTwire​=∫−2ke˙gen​​r+rC1​​ dr

    Twire​=−4ke˙gen​​r2+C1​ ln(r)+C2​

    Boundary conditions of the wire,

    T(r1​)=T1​

    drdTwire​​∣r=0​=0

    Substituting the boundary conditions and solving for the constants,

    C1​=0

    C2​=4ke˙gen​​r1​2+T1​

    Temperature distribution across the wire,

    Twire​=4ke˙gen​​(r1​2−r2)+T1​

    Conduction in the ceramic

    Applying the heat conduction equation,

    ρc∂t∂T​=r1​∂r∂​(kr∂r∂T​)+r21​∂ϕ∂​(k∂ϕ∂T​)+∂z∂​(k∂z∂T​)+e˙gen​

    0=r1​drd​(krdrdTwire​​)

    0=drd​(rdrdTceramic​​)

    Integrating once,

    rdrdTceramic​​=C1​

    drdTceramic​​=rC1​​

    Integrating twice,

    ∫dTceramic​=∫rC1​​ dr

    Tceramic​=C1​ ln(r)+C2​

    Boundary conditions of the ceramic,

    T(r1​)=T1​

    T(r2​)=Ts​=318 K

    Substituting the boundary conditions,

    T1​=C1​ ln(r1​)+C2​

    Ts​=C1​ ln(r2​)+C2​

    Solving for the constants,

    C1​=ln(r2​/r1​)Ts​−T1​​

    C2​=T1​−ln(r2​/r1​)Ts​−T1​​⋅ln(r1​)

    Temperature distribution across ceramic,

    Tceramic​=ln(r2​/r1​)Ts​−T1​​⋅ln(r)+T1​−ln(r2​/r1​)Ts​−T1​​⋅ln(r1​)

    Tceramic​=ln(r2​/r1​)Ts​−T1​​[ln(r)−ln(r1​)]+T1​

    Tceramic​=ln(r2​/r1​)ln(r/r1​)​(Ts​−T1​)+T1​

    At the interface,

    q˙​cond,wire​=q˙​cond,ceramic​

    −kdrdTwire​​​r=r1​​=−kdrdTceramic​​​r=r1​​

    −k(−2ke˙gen​​r1​)=−k[ln(r2​/r1​)Ts​−T1​​]r1​1​

    2e˙gen​​r1​=r1​kceramic​​[ln(r2​/r1​)T1​−Ts​​]

    Substituting the given values into the above,

    250×106​(0.002)=0.0021.2​[ln(0.007/0.002)T1​−318​]

    T1​=422.40 K=149.40°C

    Temperature at the center of the wire, where r=0,

    Twire​=4(15)50×106​(0.002)2+422.40

    Twire​=425.73 K=152.73°C

    Note that temperature at the center of the wire
    is slightly higher than that at the interface.
